w: What's tested His labeled Sertoli cell drawing, which he said is on the exam: every label from the basal lamina to the lumen, and the basal versus the adluminal compartment How the testis and its seminiferous tubules are organized, and where each cell sits Sertoli cells: their shape, the blood-testis barrier and its two compartments, and their jobs LH and FSH: which cell each acts on, what that cell makes, and the feedback that turns each one down Spermatogenesis: the terms, the three kinds of spermatogonia, meiosis, spermiogenesis and spermiation Leydig cells: where they are and when they make testosterone The ducts in order, the lining of each, and the two parts of the spermatic cord he said to know The epididymis: its lining and its three jobs, including how sperm mature there The seminal vesicles, prostate and bulbourethral glands: what each adds to semen, and why an enlarged prostate makes urinating hard The penis: the corpora cavernosa and the corpus spongiosum, how erection happens, and "point and shoot" Dr. Herr, the course director, gave this histology lecture on Friday, November 6, and these notes follow his recording and his slides. He follows the sperm from where they are made, through the ducts that carry them, past the glands that add the fluid, to the penis. Two things he said about the exam. One drawing is on it: the labeled Sertoli cell figure ("this image is actually on your exam ... you'll be able to answer at least one question, if not a few"), covered under Sertoli cells below. And he will not test stained micrographs: "I'm not going to test you on any specific images that are stained images, but you will see cartoon images." So learn what each structure is, where it sits and what it does, and know the drawings; don't memorize how a stain looks. The four parts of the system His overview table splits the male reproductive system into four parts. The testes are the gonads, where sperm develop by spermatogenesis and spermiogenesis. An extensive duct system, made of the intratesticular ducts and the excretory ducts, collects, stores and transports the sperm, from the testes into the pelvis and on to the urethra. The accessory glands (seminal vesicles, prostate and bulbourethral glands) secrete fluids that provide nutrients and supply the energy and lubricants for delivering the sperm. The penis is the copulatory organ. How the testis is built Each testis is wrapped in a thick capsule, the tunica albuginea. Septa run in from it and divide the testis into about 250 pyramid-shaped compartments called lobules. Each lobule holds several seminiferous tubules: blind-ended, highly coiled tubules surrounded by loose, vascular connective tissue. That connective tissue between the tubules is where the Leydig cells live. Keep that location in mind, because it is the first look-alike of the lecture: Leydig cells are outside the tubules. The tubules are long. Each is highly convoluted, 30 to 70 centimeters long and about 250 micrometers across, and there are roughly 1,000 of them in each testis, about half a kilometer of tubule in all. Sperm are made in the seminiferous tubules, leave through straight ducts into the rete testis, then pass through the efferent ductules, which join the epididymis. His labeled cross-section marks six things to find: spermatogonia at the base of the tubule, primary spermatocytes, late spermatids near the lumen, Sertoli cells, interstitial cells of Leydig outside the tubule, and peritubular myoid cells. The outer wall of each tubule is connective tissue with peritubular myoid cells in it. Inside the wall, the seminiferous epithelium, also called the germinal epithelium, is several layers thick and contains just two kinds of cells: Sertoli cells and spermatogenic cells. Interstitium, between the tubules Loose, vascular connective tissue with the Leydig cells Tubule wall Connective tissue and peritubular myoid cells Seminiferous epithelium Sertoli cells and spermatogenic cells, several layers thick Lumen Late spermatids and released sperm Both named cells are eponyms, and he pointed out the pair: Sertoli is inside the tubule, Leydig outside it. You may also see their newer names, sustentacular and interstitial cells. Temperature and output The testes descend into the scrotum during fetal development, and that matters: normal spermatogenesis needs a lower temperature than the body's. In class he said only "lower"; his slide puts it at about 35 degrees Celsius rather than the body's 37. Dr. Madison's physiology lecture gives about 34 degrees for the same point; both put it a few degrees below body temperature, so match each number to its lecture. A testis that stays in the abdomen is too warm to make sperm normally. Healthy testes form about 200 million sperm a day. The spermatogenic cells you will find are the spermatogonia, the spermatocytes and the spermatids. LH, FSH and the feedback loops Two hormones from the anterior pituitary run the testis, and each has its own target cell. He went over this twice ("you've heard it a lot, but here it is again"). Luteinizing hormone, LH, binds receptors on the Leydig cells and starts their production of testosterone, which stimulates sperm development. Follicle-stimulating hormone, FSH, acts on the Sertoli cells and stimulates them to make androgen-binding protein, ABP, which helps keep testosterone concentrated inside the seminiferous tubules. Each hormone also has a brake. Testosterone lowers LH secretion through a negative feedback loop. Inhibin, made by the Sertoli cells, blocks the release of FSH from the anterior pituitary. So a man who takes testosterone from outside switches his own LH down, and his Leydig cells lose their stimulus. LH Leydig cells Testosterone, which stimulates sperm development Testosterone lowers LH FSH Sertoli cells Androgen-binding protein, which keeps testosterone high in the tubules Inhibin from Sertoli cells blocks FSH Learn the pairs as two chains: LH, Leydig, testosterone; FSH, Sertoli, androgen-binding protein and inhibin. A question that pairs LH with Sertoli cells, or inhibin with LH, has crossed the chains. Sertoli cells The Sertoli cell, or sustentacular cell, is named for Enrico Sertoli. His one-word summary: Sertoli cells are "the refrigerator." They make the secretions that nourish the developing sperm and help transport them. Their basic shape is columnar, and each one reaches all the way from the basement membrane to the lumen of the tubule. Its nucleus is generally ovoid. The germ cells develop against and between neighboring Sertoli cells, which is how the Sertoli cell can hold them and feed them. Near their bases, in the basolateral region, neighboring Sertoli cells reach out and touch, joined by occluding, or tight, junctions that form a junctional complex. (Once in class he called them gap junctions; his slide and the rest of the lecture say occluding junctions, and that is the answer.) These junctions divide the tubule into two compartments: a basal compartment next to the basement membrane, and an adluminal compartment, "adluminal" meaning near the lumen. "You need to know the difference between those two," he said. The tight junctions are the blood-testis barrier, and its purpose is to protect the developing gametes from the immune system, which would otherwise attack these rapidly dividing cells. The spermatogonia sit in the basal compartment. Once a type B spermatogonium becomes a primary spermatocyte, it moves straight into the adluminal compartment, behind the barrier, so the spermatocytes and spermatids develop where the immune system cannot reach them. The drawing on the exam. His cartoon of two Sertoli cells is the image he said is on the exam, so learn its labels in order from the outside of the tubule to the lumen: the basal lamina; a type A spermatogonium and a type B spermatogonium, both in the basal compartment; the junctional complex between the two Sertoli cells; then, past it, a primary spermatocyte, an early spermatid, and a late spermatid up at the lumen, all in the adluminal compartment. The Sertoli cells themselves run the whole height of the drawing. Sertoli cells respond to FSH. His slide lists their functions: Physical and nutritional support of the developing germ cells. Phagocytosis of the cytoplasm shed as the round spermatid becomes sperm-shaped. Making and releasing androgen-binding protein, which helps raise and hold testosterone in the tubules. Making and releasing anti-Müllerian hormone, which prevents development of the Müllerian duct, the precursor of the female reproductive tract. In his words, it "keeps a male a male." Making and releasing inhibin, which blocks FSH release by the anterior pituitary, their part in the negative feedback. Two more facts set Sertoli cells apart. They do not divide in the mature testis, and they are resistant to heat, ionizing radiation and various toxic agents. So when the germ cells are lost, to heat or radiation or drugs, the Sertoli cells are often what remains lining the tubules. Last, the location: Sertoli cells are inside the seminiferous tubules. Leydig cells The interstitial cells of Leydig, named for Franz Leydig, sit outside the seminiferous tubules, in the loose connective tissue between them. They secrete testosterone at three times in life: during embryonic development, at sexual maturity, and throughout adult life to maintain spermatogenesis. They are the target of LH. Where Inside the tubule, basement membrane to lumen Outside the tubule, in the interstitium Hormone it answers FSH LH What it makes Androgen-binding protein, inhibin, anti-Müllerian hormone Testosterone Other jobs Supports and feeds germ cells, phagocytoses shed cytoplasm, forms the blood-testis barrier Testosterone in the embryo, at maturity and to keep spermatogenesis going Tough to kill Does not divide in the adult; resists heat, radiation and toxins Not described The third cell outside the epithelium is the peritubular myoid cell, and it is in the tubule's own wall, not out in the interstitium. So, from outside in: Leydig cells between the tubules, myoid cells in the wall, Sertoli cells and germ cells in the epithelium. Spermatogenesis: the terms His terms slide is worth knowing word for word, because the names look so alike. Spermatogenesis The whole process, from germ cell to mature sperm (spermatozoa) Spermatocytogenesis Spermatogonia differentiate into primary spermatocytes Meiosis Diploid primary spermatocytes reduce their chromosomes, forming haploid spermatids Spermiogenesis Spermatids transform into spermatozoa Spermiation The sperm is released from the Sertoli cell; excess cytoplasm stays behind Capacitation Conditioning in the female tract, needed before a sperm can fertilize He said spermatogenesis takes an estimated 74 days, "so it's not an immediate thing"; Dr. Madison's physiology lecture says the spermatids mature for about two months. All its stages happen in the seminiferous tubules, but at any one spot along a tubule the process is at one stage, and the stage changes along the length of the tubule. So in a cross-section, different tubules show different numbers of cells at each stage: one may be crowded with late spermatids while its neighbor holds mostly spermatocytes. That is normal, not damage. His next slide is titled the clonal nature of spermatogenesis: the cells that come from one spermatogonium develop together as a group. Sperm are not finished when they leave the tubule. Their maturation is completed in the epididymis, and even then they must be conditioned in the female tract, a process called capacitation, before they can fertilize an ovum. As he put it, the process really ends in the female tract, where the sperm's cap, the acrosome, has to be able to come off so the haploid sperm can join the haploid egg. Spermatogonia: three kinds Spermatogonia are small cells at the base of the tubule, in the basal compartment. At puberty, under the influence of testosterone, they enter the cell cycle. He gave three categories, and the exam can describe their nuclei: Dark type A Reserve stem cells Oval to flattened, with a peripheral nucleolus and a nuclear vacuole More dark A and pale A Pale type A Progenitor cells Lighter, rich in euchromatin, with a central nucleolus and no vacuole More pale A and type B Type B Differentiating cells Not described on his slide Primary spermatocytes, which move straight into the adluminal compartment The vacuole is the quickest tell: a nuclear vacuole and a peripheral nucleolus mean dark type A; no vacuole, a central nucleolus and a pale nucleus mean pale type A. Then meiosis, the division that reproductive cells add to ordinary mitosis. The primary spermatocyte starts out diploid. The first meiotic division makes two secondary spermatocytes, and the second meiotic division makes the spermatids, which are haploid, so they can later combine with a haploid egg. The spermatids then differentiate into spermatozoa. Spermiogenesis: spermatid to spermatozoon Spermiogenesis is the remodeling of a round spermatid into a spermatozoon, with no more cell division. The spermatid discards much of its cytoplasm, rearranges its organelles and forms a flagellum: The nucleus elongates, condenses and is reshaped into the main bulk of the sperm head. The Golgi apparatus coalesces and migrates to the top of the nucleus to form the acrosomal cap, the acrosome. The mitochondria gather in the middle piece, where their ATP powers the tail. A flagellum forms. The finished sperm has a head, a neck and a tail. He lists three to four phases, depending on whether the cap and acrosomal phases are counted separately: the Golgi phase, the cap or acrosomal phase, and the maturation phase. The process ends with spermiation, the release of the sperm from the Sertoli cell. The excess cytoplasm stays behind, and his best guess is that the Sertoli cell phagocytoses it, which fits its job of phagocytosing the cytoplasm shed during sperm development. The duct system, in order Sperm leave the testis through the intratesticular ducts and then the excretory ducts. Intratesticular ducts: the seminiferous tubules, then the tubuli recti, or straight tubules, then the rete testis, then the efferent ductules, the ductuli efferentes. Excretory ducts: the duct of the epididymis, then the ductus deferens, or vas deferens (he uses the names interchangeably), then the ejaculatory duct, then the urethra of the penis. His overview slide shortens this and calls the straight ducts the rete testis; his duct slide separates them. Learn the longer version: tubuli recti first, then the rete testis. Watch the two look-alike names too. In his overview he once said the rete testis connects to the "ductus deferens," which leads into the epididymis; he meant the ductus efferentes, and he gives the right order later in the lecture. The efferent ductules come before the epididymis; the ductus deferens comes after it. The intratesticular ducts The tubuli recti, or straight tubules, are the ducts that lead out of the seminiferous tubules. They empty into the rete testis, which sits in the mediastinum of the testis: a network of sinusoid-like channels lined by cuboidal epithelium. From the rete testis, 10 to 12 efferent ductules run to the epididymis. The efferent ductules have a lining you can recognize: patches of non-ciliated simple cuboidal cells alternate with patches of ciliated simple columnar cells, so the inner border looks uneven. Each cell type has a job. The non-ciliated cells absorb fluid coming down from the seminiferous tubules, recycling it. The ciliated cells beat to move the spermatozoa toward the epididymis. These are true, motile cilia, unlike the stereocilia further down the line. The epididymis The epididymis sits on top of the testis. Its duct is highly coiled, about 4 to 6 meters of duct packed into a small organ, so one section cuts it many times. It is lined by pseudostratified columnar epithelium with two kinds of cells. Basal cells are the precursors of the columnar cells. Columnar cells carry stereocilia on their apical surface: long, nonmotile microvilli, not true cilia. They don't move; they are there to absorb fluid from the lumen. The columnar cells also take up and digest the residual bodies, the cytoplasm eliminated during spermatogenesis, and secrete glycerophosphocholine, which inhibits capacitation, because capacitation should wait until the sperm reach the female tract. Around the duct, an inner circular and an outer longitudinal layer of muscle contract to move the contents along. The epididymis has three main functions: Maturation, over 2 to 12 days: the sperm's chromatin is stabilized, its plasma membrane changes (his slide: its surface charge), it acquires new surface proteins, and it becomes motile, gaining forward motility. Storage of sperm until ejaculation. Transport of sperm toward the ductus deferens, by peristalsis to the storage region in the tail. Capacitation is not one of the three. It happens later, in the female tract, and the epididymis actively holds it back. And note the timing: about 74 days of spermatogenesis in the tubules, then 2 to 12 days of maturation in the epididymis. Cilia or stereocilia: the look-alike linings Several of these ducts share a lining, so tell them apart by the apical surface and the wall. Rete testis Cuboidal Not described A network of channels in the mediastinum Efferent ductules Non-ciliated cuboidal alternating with ciliated columnar Motile cilia Uneven border; 10 to 12 ducts Epididymis Pseudostratified columnar, with basal cells Stereocilia One coiled duct cut many times, full of sperm Vas deferens Pseudostratified columnar Stereocilia A straight tube with a thick muscular wall Seminal vesicle Pseudostratified columnar Not described A coiled gland with yellow lipochrome pigment Vas deferens, spermatic cord and ejaculatory duct The ductus deferens, or vas deferens, is a straight tube with a thick muscular wall; in a donor, he said, it feels firm, like the tip of a shoelace. Its mucosa is lined, like the epididymis, by pseudostratified columnar epithelium with stereocilia; the straight course and the thick muscle tell them apart. It runs up into the pelvis and around the ureter at the back of the bladder. The vas is only one part of the spermatic cord; the cord also carries the vessels and nerves. Of its other parts, "the only two components that I really think you should know about" are the testicular artery, which supplies the testis with blood, and the pampiniform plexus of veins. Pampiniform means formed like the tendrils of a vine that reach out and wrap around whatever it grows on. The spermatic cord is where the vas is cut in a vasectomy. Near its end the vas swells into an ampulla. The duct of the seminal vesicle then joins it, and from there on it is the ejaculatory duct, which runs through the prostate and empties into the prostatic urethra. (His excretory duct slide says the vas itself empties into the prostatic urethra; it gets there through the ejaculatory duct.) His prostate figure also labels the prostatic utricle; he said that image "has no relevance to you." Because the glands join the tract beyond the spermatic cord, a vasectomy removes the sperm from semen but leaves nearly all of its volume. The seminal vesicles The seminal vesicles are coiled tubular glands about 15 centimeters long. The lumen is lined by pseudostratified columnar epithelium, over a fibroelastic lamina propria, with inner circular and outer longitudinal smooth muscle. Their secretion makes up most of the semen, about 70 percent of its volume, and it is rich in fructose, the main energy source for sperm, along with prostaglandins and proteins: supplies packed for the journey. Dr. Madison's physiology lecture gives an estimated 50 to 80 percent for the same fluid, so 70 percent sits inside his range. Their cells contain a yellowish lipochrome pigment, and that gives them forensic importance: the pigment fluoresces under ultraviolet light, which helps identify semen stains. He said he is not concerned that you know the staining of the seminal vesicle or prostate sections. The prostate The prostate is wrapped around the urethra, and he flagged what that means for a patient: someone who has trouble urinating, or takes a long time to urinate, may have a prostate compressing the urethra. It is 30 to 50 compound tubuloalveolar glands, arranged in three sets: mucosal glands nearest the urethra, then submucosal, then the main glands on the outside. (He has seen the prostate divided into zones several other ways; this is the one on his slide.) Its epithelium is simple or pseudostratified columnar, set in a fibromuscular stroma. The cells have the organelles of a protein-secreting cell: rough endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi and secretory granules. His slide lists a few things the prostate produces: Fibrinolysin, a proteinase; its secretions are rich in proteolytic enzymes. It is the main source of citric acid and acid phosphatase in semen. Dr. Madison's physiology lecture also lists citric acid among the seminal vesicles' products; on Dr. Herr's slide the prostate is the main source. Prostaglandins and amylase. Prostate-specific antigen, PSA, a clinically important tumor marker, often raised in certain forms of prostate cancer. Prostatic fluid is the first portion of the ejaculate. Urine is slightly acidic, and acid would kill sperm, so the prostate's slightly alkaline fluid reduces the acidity of the urethra. It also helps dilute, or liquefy, the semen and provides a medium for the sperm. The prostate is active all the time: it secretes up to 2 milliliters a day, which usually leaves in the urine. In the gland lumens you may see prostatic concretions, the corpora amylacea. They are calcified glycoproteins, they increase with age, and their significance is unknown. The bulbourethral glands The bulbourethral glands are also called Cowper's glands, named for William Cowper, an anatomist known for his drawings. They are small, bulb-shaped glands beside the membranous urethra, in the muscle that stretches between the pelvic bones. They make a thick, slippery mucous secretion rich in galactose and sialic acid, and they empty it into the penile urethra. The secretion lubricates the urethra, and it precedes the emission of semen: the bulbourethral glands contract first, the prostate's fluid comes as the first portion of the ejaculate, and then comes the fluid of the seminal vesicles with the sperm from the ductus deferens. The one thing to take from his bulbourethral slide is the skeletal muscle between the secretory units. He asked the class whether skeletal muscle is under autonomic or somatic control: somatic, so these glands can be voluntarily controlled. Structure Coiled tubular glands, about 15 cm 30 to 50 compound tubuloalveolar glands in three sets, wrapped around the urethra Small, bulb-shaped mucous glands Lining and wall Pseudostratified columnar; smooth muscle, inner circular and outer longitudinal Simple or pseudostratified columnar; fibromuscular stroma Skeletal muscle between the units (somatic control) Key products Fructose, prostaglandins, proteins Citric acid, acid phosphatase, fibrinolysin, PSA, amylase, prostaglandins Galactose and sialic acid When and how much About 70 percent of the volume The first portion of the ejaculate Before the emission of semen Slide clue Yellow lipochrome pigment Concretions (corpora amylacea) Skeletal muscle Semen Semen is the sperm plus the fluid: fluid from the testis and the secretory products of the epididymis, the vas deferens, the prostate, the seminal vesicles and the bulbourethral glands. Its prostaglandins influence sperm transit in both the male and the female reproductive tracts. An average ejaculate is about 3 milliliters, with up to 100 million sperm per milliliter, and about 25 percent of the sperm in any ejaculate are abnormal, immotile, or both. The penis and erection A cross-section of the penis shows the fascia on the outside, the dorsal vein and, deeper, the deep dorsal vein, with arteries and nerves. Inside are the erectile bodies, wrapped in a thick tunica albuginea. "Corpora" means bodies and "cavernosa" means full of caverns: there are two corpora cavernosa, each with a central artery (the deep artery of the penis). The erectile tissue is made of trabeculae with cavernous spaces, or sinusoids, between them. The urethra runs instead in the corpus spongiosum, which is softer and fills with far less blood. That keeps the urethra open, so semen can pass during erection. "If we had a corpus cavernosum around the urethra, there wouldn't be many human beings." Erection results from relaxation of the trabecular and arterial smooth muscle: the central arteries dilate and the cavernous spaces of the two corpora cavernosa fill with blood. His summary slide adds the third step, compression of the venous outflow against the tunica albuginea: the swelling tissue presses the draining veins against the unyielding tunica, so blood that has come in cannot get out, and the tissue stays rigid. Relax, fill, trap. The common mistake is to think the smooth muscle contracts. It relaxes. His slide's flaccid-and-erect blood supply figure (helicine arteries from the deep artery filling the cavernous spaces, nutritive arteries to the trabeculae, arteriovenous shunts, the deep veins) is one he said "you don't need to know ... necessarily." To finish, he passed on his own histology teacher's mnemonic: "point and shoot." Erection, the pointing, is parasympathetic; ejaculation, the shooting, is sympathetic.
